chapter: London and return to New York
title: Emil Christian's letter and why New Orleans men could not play the Dixieland rhythm
summary: A 1920 letter from Christian asks for Dixieland-style players rather than New York men. La Rocca argues no New Orleans band had the original band's rhythm and says laws in 1921 forced the band off Broadway.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yes that's right. We'll keep it now. This is a letter from Emil Christian and it says I would like Philip Napoleon on cornet and Johnny Costello on clarinet. The boys I was working with because they have more of an idea what I want and they can play all the Dixieland numbers because I'll know we'll get some requests for them. It's signed on the back here. Sincerely, Emil Christian, 2 Bagley Street, Tidingham Court Road, Apartment 1, London, England. And I don't see the date. Let me think. It's on the 1st. The date is September 6, 1920.

Now from this letter you'll see this is a New Orleans man. I could have had him shopping. I could have got him Gardena, Giardina, Tony Giardina was around New York doing nothing. And I had contacted these men finally. But he wanted men who copied from the Dixieland records. We'll go to show you that even the New Orleans boys didn't want the boys from New Orleans because they didn't know the rhythm. That is the truth that I am sitting here and telling you that no New Orleans band played the rhythm that was contained in the original Dixieland jazz band recording. They had to acquire it by listening to it. Well the New Orleans boys were setting away of their own. They couldn't see and they couldn't feel. The same as the Negroes that came. They thought they had the rhythm. They were making ta-ta-ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Well that is an ending I make on many of my pieces played eight years before them. Ta-ta-ta-da-da-da-da-da-da. Tip된 stuff with a saxophone. They forced us to use a saxophone because throughout the country there was something about eliminating jazz because it was ruining the morals of the girls. Well we made these records, they sold, sold into millions but they were not the same as the other record. You take a man playing from the north who had not copied the style although he was a technical man. There was no better saxophone player than him yet he couldn't fit in the band properly. It broke up a sort of the rhythm of the band. A lot of people says the demise of the original Dixieland Jan was dead. No, we were forced to the wall by laws. John Rhodes Stratton went to Albany, New York in 1921 and passed laws prohibiting jazz bands from playing on Broadway. We were the only jazz band playing on Broadway. We had to give up the contract with the Father of the Bajer because we were the player the fall and winter. That was when they put Gildegary in jail for doing the shimmy. And they stopped the band at 12 o'clock.
